p:BLZ: The Central Bank of Belize issues the Belize dollar, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar. Government money it keeps has twice been found not to add up. For 2011/2012 the Auditor General reported that 25 government accounts held at the bank could not be shown to have been reconciled, and that public debt records the bank manages did not match the Accountant General's statements. The National Assembly's Joint Public Accounts Committee, on the Auditor General's report for April 2016 to March 2017, made differences between Central Bank and SmartStream balances of 42 million, 19 million, 3 million and 1.4 million dollars a priority area, and at hearings in March 2026 Auditor General Maria Rodriguez said the Central Bank accounts were not being reconciled. In August 2021 governor Gustavo Manuel Vasquez lost his post: Prime Minister John Briceño said the board had recommended he resign over a lot of policy differences, while Vasquez wrote that the Ministry of Finance had instructed his termination. De La Rue printed the 100-dollar note introduced on 4 August 2025, and Belize scores 35 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. Two careers run out of the bank and back in, Kareem Michael's through the utility Belize Electricity Limited and Marina Laetitia Murillo's through private financial-sector management.
p:BWA: The Bank of Botswana issues the pula, which it manages against the South African rand within a narrow band. One case is recorded and it ended in acquittal: a woman arrested on 17 October 2019 was accused, with others including former president Ian Khama and former intelligence head Isaac Kgosi, of stealing 100 billion pula. High Court judge Zein Kebonang acquitted her, the state withdrew a terrorism financing charge, and he found the accusations fabricated and referred the investigator for perjury prosecution; the accusations against the others remain unproven. In January 2020 the Directorate of Public Prosecutions, headed by Stephen Tiroyakgosi, called in governor Moses Pelaelo over that sum, and Tiroyakgosi said Pelaelo told them there is no money missing, with the investigation continuing. In May 2019 the Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime confirmed it was investigating unaccounted-for funds on government accounts at the bank, after the Auditor General reported 22 billion pula unaccounted for. Linah Kelebogile Mohohlo, Governor from 20 October 1999 until October 2016, worked at the International Monetary Fund from 1994 to 1996. De La Rue printed the 10 pula polymer note issued on 1 February 2018, and Botswana scores 26 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:LTU: Lithuania uses the euro, so the European Central Bank, not the Bank of Lithuania, sets interest rates, for the 21 countries that share the currency. Lithuania's own case ended in acquittal. An official who monitored the commercial bank Snoras was sacked in November 2011 and charged with letting Snoras keep information from the bank's leadership; a Vilnius court annulled his March 2014 conviction, finding no crime, and that ruling can still be appealed. In May 2012 a parliamentary commission chaired by Valentinas Mazuronis found the bank had shut Snoras down too fast and with too little reasoning, the takeover of its shares and the bankruptcy proceedings both hasty. Two further cases sit at the European Central Bank. In case 1697/2016/ANA the European Ombudsman found maladministration and in January 2018 recommended that president Mario Draghi give up his Group of Thirty membership; the bank declined. On 18 May 2015 one of its officials, Cœuré, told a private London event that it would bring forward its asset purchases, and the speech was published only the next morning, which the bank blamed on an internal procedure error. Six of that bank's officials have moved to or from private finance, Otmar Issing to a loose advisory position with Goldman Sachs in 2006. Lithuania's 5.8 tonnes of gold are all held at the Bank of England, and it scores 22 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:RWA: The National Bank of Rwanda issues the Rwandan franc, which in practice follows a crawling peg against the US dollar, meaning the rate is allowed to drift slowly in a managed way. In November 2012 the Senate summoned governor Claver Gatete, who appeared with finance minister John Rwangombwa, over the franc's slide after it weakened 1.3 percent against the dollar in the first half of the year; Gatete put it down to speculation, and said the bank had put 327.8 million US dollars into the market since 2011. One case is recorded: the bank lost 63 million Rwandan francs from deposit accounts in early 2014 in a fraud reported to involve its own staff, and its information technology director said the suspects had manipulated its internal security system before taking the cash. One person was arrested and the file went to the Prosecutor General, while police said the main suspect was believed to have fled to Uganda; the matter is under investigation, so nothing in it is proven. De La Rue printed the 2,000-franc note introduced on 3 September 2024. Rwangombwa was Governor from 2013 until February 2025 and came from government, as Minister of Finance and Economic Planning from 2009. It scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:COM: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it: a monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. It set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Two governments also fill its board. Under statutes signed in Paris on 22 April 2008 it had at most eight members, half named by each government, the Governor by the President of the Union of the Comoros. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France names two of the six board members, two of the four members of the banking supervision committee and two of the four members of the committee that sets monetary policy and manages reserves. The notes are printed at the Banque de France. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. It holds no gold, Mazars Fivoarana audited its 2024 accounts, and it scores 65 of 100, the highest of the 194 places with a figure.
p:MAC: Macao's money, the pataca, is issued by the Monetary Authority of Macao, and in December 2025 it was held at a fixed rate against the United States dollar. Its law leaves it little independence: 0.271 of 1 on one index, the lowest of 155 places, and the head of the executive appoints its board. That still holds. On 26 June 2025 Chief Executive Sam Hou Fai appointed Vong Sin Man, a worker of the Statistics and Census Service, to the board for 1 July to 31 December 2025, under the Authority's statute of 11 March 1996. One case is documented, an administrative finding by a foreign regulator rather than a criminal conviction: on 15 September 2005 the US Treasury named Banco Delta Asia, a bank licensed and supervised in Macao, a primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN proposed cutting it off from US correspondent accounts. Treasury said the bank had served North Korean government agencies and front companies for more than 20 years, and alleged that senior officials accepted large cash deposits, including counterfeit US currency, and agreed to circulate them; the bank denied wrongdoing. The 1,000-pataca note of the Bank of China Macau series is printed by Hong Kong Note Printing Limited, and Macao scores 34 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:DJI: The Central Bank of Djibouti, created in 1977, runs what is called a currency board: the Djibouti franc is held at 1 US dollar to 177.721 francs and backed entirely by US dollars, so the bank cannot issue francs without dollars behind them. The franc itself was created in March 1949, outside the franc zone. The executive fills the bank's board: under the statutes set by law no. 118/AN/11/6eme L of 22 January 2011 it is the Governor and six administrators appointed by decree, so every seat but the Governor's is a government appointment. The bank's own 2024 annual report sets out that composition and cites the 2011 law, so the arrangement still stands. The independence written into its law scores 0.698 of 1, where 1 means the bank holds the power rather than the government. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index. It scores 60 of 100, the second highest of the 194 places with a figure, with money-laundering risk in its banks rated 6.93 of 10. Deloitte Côte d'Ivoire audited the 2021 accounts.
p:PSE: The Palestine Monetary Authority is the monetary authority of Palestine, which has no currency listed here; its exchange-rate classification reads no separate legal tender, or currency union. The head of state names its board. On 4 May 2026 President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree reconstituting the board of directors, acting on a recommendation from the Cabinet and from the Authority's Governor. Three of the eight seats are held by virtue of law: the Governor as chairman, the Deputy Governor, and a representative of the Ministry of Finance, named as Majdi Al-Hassan. The law that created the bank in 1997 gives it a legal independence score of 0.435 of 1, ranking 155 of 191. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index. Government pressure was reported in none of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018. The bank scores 41 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption in the country.
p:BTN: Bhutan's central bank is the Royal Monetary Authority, which issues the ngultrum and keeps it pegged, or fixed, to the Indian rupee; the rupee circulates in the country as well. Its own law lets the government direct it: section 149 of the Royal Monetary Authority Act of Bhutan 2010, in force from 22 June 2010, lets the Royal Government issue directives it considers necessary in the public interest, after consulting the Governor and reporting them to Parliament. Four of the Board's seven members are appointed by the Government, one of them from the Ministry of Finance, and the Royal Government sets the Governor's salary and the board members' fees. The Governor is appointed by the Druk Gyalpo on the Prime Minister's recommendation and may be removed the same way, but only on a committee finding of incapacity or misconduct. An anonymous informer raised a case in October 2014, and the final findings of Bhutan's Anti-Corruption Commission, covering 2014 to 2016, said a former deputy governor had allegedly forged official documents, misused power and concealed earnings from World Bank and Asian Development Bank projects. Those allegations are unproven; the case was forwarded to the Office of the Attorney General, with no later outcome. The bank scores 27 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:BMU: Bermuda's money is the Bermudian dollar, issued by the Bermuda Monetary Authority, its central bank, and in December 2025 it sat in a de facto peg to the US dollar, held at a fixed rate in practice. Independence written into law is almost absent, 0.06 of 1 and second from last of 191 places, with no reform since 1970, and the bank scores 3.5 of 15 for what it tells the public. Bermuda scores 34 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, the weakest part being secrecy, because the island's laws hide who owns money. No documented case at the bank was found, which does not prove none happened. One career move is recorded: Cheryl-Ann Lister, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of the Authority from 1999 through 2006, was appointed an independent director of AXIS Capital Holdings Limited, a Bermuda-based insurance and reinsurance group, in an announcement of 23 September 2008. The Office of the Auditor-General audits the accounts, as it did for 2021, and the notes are printed abroad: on 30 October 2024 the authority announced that its new 2 and 5 dollar notes, printed by De La Rue on polymer, would enter circulation that autumn.
p:CYM: The Cayman Islands Monetary Authority acts as the central bank of the Cayman Islands, and the currency is the Cayman Islands dollar. In June 2015 it said it would commission an internal review of local involvement in the FIFA corruption case, after the Caymanian businessman Jeffrey Webb was arrested in Switzerland on 27 May. Its managing director Cindy Scotland's husband, the former minister Mark Scotland, had worked for the Cayman Islands Football Association under Webb and was with him at the arrest, and Gloria Glidden, deputy head of the banking division, is the wife of the former minister Cline Glidden, who was also in Switzerland with Webb. Chairman George McCarthy said Scotland would remain managing director and that there was no evidence any Cayman bank had done anything wrong; the review is still under investigation. One career move runs the other way, into the authority: its own board page says director Greg Swart was managing member and chief financial officer of the alternative asset manager Farallon Capital Management LLC from 2002 to 2019, after about twelve years at Goldman Sachs. A commemorative 70-dollar note for the Platinum Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II, introduced on 12 October 2023, was printed by De La Rue, the Auditor General of the Cayman Islands audits the accounts, and the authority scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MKD: North Macedonia's money is the denar, issued by the National Bank of the Republic of North Macedonia and held in practice at a fixed rate to the euro. Its notes are printed abroad: the French firm Oberthur Fiduciaire took the 100-denar contract reported on 8 May 2026, at 59,800,000 denars or about 972,358 euros; the Russian joint-stock company Goznak printed that note in 2021 for about 400,000 euros, part of a reissue carrying the state's changed constitutional name; and De La Rue International prints the 10, 500 and 1,000 denar notes, 45 million of them at 3.775 million euros. One case, from 2017 to 2020, is unproven: an association of Eurostandard Bank depositors said the governor tipped off the finance minister and other large depositors so they could take their money out before the bank went under administration, and that financial police reports were kept secret so it could keep operating. It put Finance Minister Nina Angelovska's withdrawal at more than 200,000 euros and the loss at over 60 million euros; no charges and no official finding are reported. Two careers are on record: governor Anita Angelovska Bezhoska's, through the Ministry of Finance and the International Monetary Fund, with no private firm in it, and Dimitar Bogov's, who was chief economist of the commercial bank Stopanska Banka AD Skopje before becoming vice governor and then governor from 2011. It scores 24 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:ZMB: The Bank of Zambia issues the kwacha, which floats within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Denny Kalyalya came to the governorship in February 2015 from the World Bank Group, where he had been executive director for Africa Group One. On 22 August 2020 President Edgar Lungu dismissed him, less than a week after he warned of economic difficulties, and appointed Christopher Mvunga from the finance ministry; Kalyalya returned in October 2021. In October 2015 the Drug Enforcement Commission arrested a section officer for theft by a public servant and money laundering, accusing him of taking 43,660 US dollars and 20,335 kwacha in cash that year; he was charged, no court outcome is given, so the accusation is unproven. Of three career moves on record, one runs into a commercial bank: Austin Mwape went from deputy governor of operations to chairman of the board of Stanbic Bank Zambia, part of the Standard Bank Group, from December 2016 until 1 September 2020. The others stay in public hands, Richard Chembe's into Investrust Bank, whose largest shareholder was already the state-owned ZCCM Investments Holdings. The Heritage Series of six notes and six coins was launched on 31 March 2025, with the 10 and 20 kwacha notes on Landqart's Durasafe substrate; who printed it is not published. Zambia scores 32 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:CPV: The Bank of Cape Verde issues the escudo, and the government of Portugal guarantees it under a currency cooperation agreement signed on 13 March 1998. The rate is fixed at 110.265 Cape Verdean escudos to the euro, having started at 0.55 escudos to the Portuguese escudo. The Portuguese Treasury provides a short-term credit line of 27.5 million euros, which can rise to 45 million, with drawings capped at 5 million, and Cabo Verde must transfer reserves equal to 35 per cent of what it asks for; Banco de Portugal states the facility obliges neither it nor any euro-area institution to step in. The bank has also signed a technical assistance agreement with the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, becoming its 75th member, which is advisory work rather than management of its assets. De La Rue printed the 1,000 and 2,000 escudo notes released on 15 April 2025, and EY's Cape Verde member firm signed the auditor's report on the 2024 accounts without qualifications, on negative equity of 622,855 thousand escudos. No case at the bank is documented, which is not proof none happened. It scores 47 of 100, ranking 13 of 194, with money issued, backed or fixed from abroad the main reason.
